title: Limiting factors and rate of photosynthesis; Link reaction and Krebs cycle; Anaerobic respiration; Respiratory substrates and RQ; respirometers
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RS02#t2 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t4 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RS02#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PS04#N.3, RS02#N.3a, RS04#N.3a, RS05#N.7, PS04#N.8, RS02#N.5, RS04#N.11a, RS05#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Matrix
items.clue: The fluid enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.label: Outer membrane
items.clue: Smooth boundary layer that encloses the whole mitochondrion.

items.label: Intermembrane space
items.clue: Narrow gap between the outer and inner boundaries of a mitochondrion.

items.label: Cristae
items.clue: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, holding the electron carriers.

questions.stem: Pondweed submerged in water at 25 °C with the carbon dioxide concentration of ordinary air was exposed to increasing light intensity. The rate of photosynthesis rose at first and then levelled off, staying constant however much the light intensity was increased. Which change is most likely to raise the rate at this plateau?

options.text: Moving the lamp even closer, so that the light intensity becomes higher still.
Adding sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water to raise the carbon dioxide concentration.
Nothing, because the plateau is the maximum rate of which the plant is capable.
Adding more water to the beaker, since water is a reactant in photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction of aerobic cell respiration?

options.text: It enters the Krebs cycle directly, where it combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
It reacts with oxygen in the matrix, forming carbon dioxide and a two-carbon acetyl group that enters the cycle.
It is oxidised and decarboxylated to a 2C acetyl group, which coenzyme A carries to the Krebs cycle.
It is bound by coenzyme A, the enzyme that catalyses its conversion into citrate in the matrix.

questions.explanation: Pyruvate loses carbon dioxide (decarboxylation) and hydrogen (oxidation, reducing NAD). The acetyl group is bound to coenzyme A and transferred to the cycle.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?

options.text: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
To oxidise pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.
To convert pyruvate into a form able to enter the mitochondria.
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.

questions.explanation: Reducing pyruvate to lactate turns reduced NAD back to NAD. Glycolysis, which needs NAD, continues with a net two ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?

options.text: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen given out per gram per minute
0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute

questions.explanation: The fall in volume equals the oxygen consumed, as the alkali removes carbon dioxide. 1.2 ÷ 10 ÷ 5.0 = 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹.

questions.stem: A student places a lamp at different distances from a beaker of pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution kept at 25 °C, and counts the bubbles of gas released per minute at each distance. Which correctly identifies the variables?

options.text: Independent: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: bubbles per minute; dependent: distance of lamp
Controlled variable: lamp distance; dependent: bubbles per minute
Independent: temperature of 25 °C; dependent: bubbles per minute

questions.explanation: Lamp distance is deliberately changed (it sets light intensity): independent. Bubble count is measured: dependent. Temperature and hydrogencarbonate concentration are controlled.

questions.stem: One acetyl group enters the Krebs cycle and oxaloacetate is regenerated. Which account of one turn of the cycle is correct?

options.text: Two decarboxylations give off carbon dioxide, four dehydrogenations reduce carriers, one ATP forms.
Two carbon dioxide molecules form when oxygen oxidises the carbon atoms of the acetyl group directly.
Each of the four oxidations forms one ATP directly, so the cycle yields most of the cell's ATP supply.
Only decarboxylation occurs, since no oxygen enters the matrix to oxidise any of the cycle's intermediates.

questions.explanation: Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP forms directly.

questions.stem: Crucian carp can survive for months in ice-covered ponds with no oxygen. In these conditions their muscle cells convert pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the ethanol leaves through the gills. Which statement about this anaerobic respiration is correct?

options.text: It takes place inside the mitochondria, which is where the ethanol is made.
All its ATP comes from glycolysis: far less per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Converting pyruvate to ethanol releases extra ATP, which is why the fish survives.
It still uses the small amount of oxygen that remains dissolved in the pond water.

questions.stem: Illustrative data. A student measured oxygen uptake by yeast (cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹) at five temperatures: 20 °C 0.10; 30 °C 0.19; 40 °C 0.31; 50 °C 0.26; 60 °C 0.04. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Rate rises with temperature over the whole range, so the low reading at 60 °C must be an experimental error.
Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum near 40 °C, then falls as the enzymes of respiration denature.
Above 40 °C the yeast switches to anaerobic respiration, which uses no oxygen, so oxygen uptake falls.
At 60 °C the extra carbon dioxide produced expands and pushes the liquid back, hiding the true rate.
